lines: Comparing a row to its own neighbors is one kind of question.
Now: comparing a row to the exact value another table held, at that very moment in time.
A price list doesn't store one row per sale. It stores one row per time the price changed.
So "what was the price when this order happened" isn't asking for a match. It's asking for the most recent change that had already happened by then.
Can an ordinary, equal-to-equal join answer that by itself?
answer: No. Equal-to-equal only tells it which product. It says nothing about which moment in that product's price history is the right one.
You need a second condition entirely... at or before this exact moment... and then, out of everything that qualifies, keep only the closest one.
That's a genuinely different shape of question, not just a stricter join.

lines: There are a few honest ways to answer it.
Look it up fresh, per row, with a small nested query.
Or use the same per-row trick from a few topics back... sort just that product's history, and keep the one closest match.
Or, on an engine that built this in on purpose, just say what you mean directly: join each row to its closest match in time, full stop.
All three give the identical answer. They just differ in how much the engine has to work for it, and how clearly the intent reads on the page.
Here's where this becomes more than a syntax curiosity.
Imagine training a model, and for every past example, you hand it today's current value of some signal... not the value that signal actually had, back when that example happened.
Does that model, trained that way, know something it genuinely shouldn't?
answer: Yes. It's quietly seeing the future, relative to each example it's learning from.
It looks great in testing, because the future it's peeking at is sitting right there in the training data too.
Then it ships, where the future genuinely isn't available yet... and the whole advantage evaporates.
Matching every example to the value that was actually knowable at that exact moment is the fix, by construction. That's exactly what this closest-match join enforces.

lines: One more distinction, just so the next layer doesn't get confused with this one.
Everything here tracked one clock: when something became true in the real world.
A harder version tracks two clocks at once: when it became true, and separately, when your own system actually found out about it.
Most of what you'll touch day to day only needs the one clock. Save the two-clock version for when a correction, learned late, genuinely needs to not rewrite what an earlier report already said.
So: a closest-match-in-time join is a real, different shape of question, not a stricter ordinary join.
Three honest ways to write it, same answer, different cost.
And matching to what was knowable at the time, instead of what's current now, is the whole difference between a model that works and one that only looks like it does.
Every clause so far answered what a query means.
